MUNICIPAL APPLICATION GUIDE

Dongfeng Electric Sprinkler Trucks: KT3F 4x2 and KT7A 6x4

Compare the catalogue-listed KT3F and KT7A chassis for municipal water-service routes, while confirming tank, pump, spray equipment and completed-vehicle details separately.

APPLICATION GUIDEOctober 8, 20269 min read
In this guideCatalogue configurationsRoute and duty profileTank and equipmentEnergy and chargingMunicipal operationData limitsBuyer checklistFAQ

KT3F and KT7A entries at a glance

The catalogue lists KT3F as a 4x2 sprinkler application in the 18 t GVW class. The row gives 166 / 200 kWh battery options, motor entries of 128 / 260 or 110 / 210 kW, direct drive / 4AMT, 4,500 mm wheelbase, 295/80R22.5 tyres, EBS and GB charging. KT7A is listed as a 6x4 sprinkler model in the 25 t GVW class, with 232 kWh, 164 / 308 kW output, 4AMT, 5,000 + 1,350 mm wheelbase, 295/80R22.5 tyres, EBS and GB charging.

The catalogue's 6 t / 10 t field for these rows appears under the product page's “Front / rear axle” column. It is not clearly labeled as tank volume. Therefore this guide does not describe those numbers as water capacity, axle ratings or a completed body specification. Ask the supplier to explain the field and obtain the actual water-tank volume, material, pump and spray-system schedule in writing.

GVW is gross vehicle weight, not water payload. Allowable water mass depends on completed chassis and body mass, axle loading, tank design, equipment and local requirements. Water weighs approximately one kilogram per litre under ordinary conditions, but tank volume alone still cannot establish a lawful vehicle payload. The final calculation must include the vehicle, tank, pump, piping, hose reels, crew and accessories.

Match the chassis to the route pattern

Municipal water work can include street washing, dust suppression, landscaping support, roadworks or seasonal service. Define exactly where water is collected, where it is discharged, and how often the truck returns to refill. Record each route's distance, gradient, road surface, speed, stops, traffic windows and refill location. A repeated short urban loop with a nearby water point differs from a long rural service route with sparse refill access. The planned route should include travel to and from the depot, not just the spray operation.

Walk the route with the fleet and road teams. Check width restrictions, turning areas, low structures, bridge limits, street access windows, slopes, curbside parking and places where the vehicle may have to reverse. A 6x4 chassis is not automatically the better choice because it has an additional axle, and 4x2 does not automatically mean that it can enter every narrow street. Compare overall dimensions, completed axle loads, traction needs, legal limits and the tank-body mass distribution.

Work out the day's water demand and the number of refill cycles independently from the vehicle's energy plan. The route can be constrained by water access, spray application rate, hose setup, operator time or traffic restrictions rather than battery state. Record gallons/litres consumed per route only from actual body-system data. Ask the equipment supplier for pump flow, pressure, spray pattern, controls and duty limits. The project catalogue does not supply those measurements.

For streets with frequent stop-start operation, low-speed maneuvering and a fixed service area may matter more than highway speed. For a larger service territory or heavier completed body, the 6x4 KT7A is a candidate to assess; this is not a recommendation without route and axle calculations. Use the 4x2 KT3F as a separate candidate where its 18 t GVW class, dimensions and completed body meet the task. Compare them against the same operational requirement and approved mass limits.

Specify tank, pump and spraying equipment explicitly

A sprinkler truck is a chassis plus a water-service body. Specify tank capacity, material, corrosion protection, baffles, fill connections, drain, access, pump, piping, spray bars, rear nozzles, side sprays, hose reel, controls and safety provisions with a qualified body builder. Decide whether the truck needs remote spray controls, manual hose operation or multiple delivery modes. Confirm installation mass, tank location, axle distribution, center of gravity and the water-level indication method.

Partially filled water can move during acceleration, braking and cornering. Tank design, internal baffles, fill level and driving behavior should be addressed by the body designer and operator training. Do not treat a full-water configuration and an empty tank as equivalent for handling or energy. The site and route risk assessment should consider gradients, turning, braking distance and the location of refill points. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for safe operation and maintenance.

Coordinate the body power needs with the exact chassis variant. The catalogue gives different motor and transmission entries for KT3F, and a single row does not map every combination to a specific model code. Obtain a vehicle-specific build sheet, clarify how the pump is powered and whether an electric pump or mechanical drive is included. Establish the continuous power, control, duty cycle, emergency stop and interlock requirements. Do not infer a pump rating from traction-motor power.

Confirm the completed-vehicle mass calculation with tank empty and at defined operating fill levels. Ensure axle loads remain within the approved envelope throughout water use. Ask for drawings showing tank dimensions, mounting points, ground clearance, overall height, rear overhang and service access. Recheck turning and braking after body completion rather than relying solely on the bare chassis layout.

Plan battery use around both travel and body work

The listed battery capacities are not guaranteed daily distances. Energy consumption depends on route, payload, stop-start operation, ambient conditions, cab systems and body equipment. A pump may be powered separately or through a chassis/body interface depending on the final design; the catalogue does not identify the exact pump drive or its energy consumption. Ask the vehicle and body suppliers to specify this boundary and assess total energy for the planned service shift.

Collect data during a pilot or use a validated comparable duty record. Log distance, route, water mass at departure, refill events, pump operating time, energy use, state of charge and weather. Separate driving energy from body-operation energy if the instrumentation allows. Include travel to refill, queueing, idling, cleaning and end-of-shift charging. Avoid quoting range or number of streets served from battery capacity alone.

Determine where the vehicle parks and charges between shifts. Confirm the actual GB connector and charger compatibility, charging window, site electrical capacity and backup process. Coordinate overnight charging with vehicle return, wash-down and tank maintenance. The inlet and electrical equipment need protection from water exposure consistent with the vehicle and charger instructions; have qualified professionals approve placement and procedures.

Build a dependable municipal service process

Municipal assignments often have fixed service windows, public interaction and changing road conditions. Give dispatchers a route plan, refill schedule, vehicle dimension information and a process for street closures or emergency reassignment. Drivers and operators should be trained on safe fill levels, pump controls, spray equipment, charging, water-source hygiene where relevant to the use, daily inspections and defect escalation. The applicable municipal and occupational rules must be checked locally.

Maintenance planning should include tank inspection, pump and piping, nozzle blockage, leaks, winterization where relevant, high-voltage and chassis checks, tyres, brakes and scheduled service. Agree which party services the body and which handles the vehicle. Confirm spare nozzles, hoses, seals and pump parts as well as chassis components. Before accepting a fleet, perform a body commissioning test and a route rehearsal using the completed vehicle.

Important data gaps before procurement

The catalogue does not state a confirmed tank volume, pump flow or pressure, spray width, body mass, operating range, charge time, price or warranty for the KT3F or KT7A body. It also does not map all KT3F motor combinations to model codes. The 6 t / 10 t field is ambiguous under the current displayed table labels and must not be represented as tank size. Require a clarified technical schedule before comparing quotations.

Likewise, a stated GVW class is not the payload of water. Obtain a completed vehicle mass and axle-load statement at empty and full tank conditions. Verify destination requirements, charging compatibility, body installation and service coverage. A general catalogue image is not evidence that it depicts either sprinkler model.

Electric sprinkler truck procurement checklist

  • Define service purpose, route area, working hours, refill points and water demand.
  • Compare KT3F 4x2 and KT7A 6x4 dimensions, GVW and completed mass for the route.
  • Request the exact KT3F model code and motor/transmission combination.
  • Specify tank volume, material, baffles, pump, flow, pressure, spray equipment and controls.
  • Obtain empty/full axle loads, body drawings, center-of-gravity and legal payload review.
  • Clarify the catalogue's 6 t / 10 t field with the supplier; do not infer its meaning.
  • Estimate travel and pump energy from actual duty data, then set a practical reserve.
  • Confirm GB charger compatibility, safe wash-down procedure, service and spare parts.

Visit the electric special vehicle catalogue, compare the KT1D municipal sweeper guide, and review charging compatibility questions. To discuss a fleet, share the route, water requirement, body concept and charging location.

Frequently asked questions

Which is larger, KT3F or KT7A?

The catalogue lists KT3F as 4x2 / 18 t GVW and KT7A as 6x4 / 25 t GVW. These are chassis classes, not a statement of tank capacity or payload.

How large is the water tank?

The available model rows do not clearly state a tank volume. The 6 t / 10 t field is displayed under front/rear axle, so request clarification and a body-specific tank specification.

Can the listed kWh predict a daily route?

No. Route energy depends on distance, water mass, stops, pump operation, conditions and reserve. Use a measured duty cycle and supplier guidance.

Does GB charging mean any site charger will work?

No. Verify inlet, protocol, electrical limits and charger acceptance for the exact vehicle and installed charging equipment.
